title: Choosing a Cytogenetic Test: Karyotype, FISH, Microarray and Prenatal cfDNA
summary: Match karyotype, FISH and chromosomal microarray to the question asked, state what each cannot detect, apply the ISCN clone rule, and explain why cell-free DNA screening needs diagnostic confirmation.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 71 Hits 4, 5 and 10 and Traps 1, 2 and 5. Checked against Miller 2010 (abstract only; full text not accessible), Rohani 2018, Wan 2014, Poulton & Hui 2025 and Santoli 2025. Not taught: the reviewer’s high-resolution karyotype ~3 Mb and FISH ~150 kb figures (Rohani gives FISH/SKY > 1–2 Mb; FISH resolution depends on the probe), “score 15–20 cells”, and Hit 11’s procedure timings, loss rates and NIPS accuracy (not in the sources read).

objectives: Match karyotype, FISH and microarray to a clinical question.
State the main blind spot of each method.
Apply the clone rule and the screening-vs-diagnosis rule for cell-free DNA.

scenes.title: Three requests, three different tests
scenes.altText: Three request slips on the cytogenetics bench (invented): (1) a 4-year-old with unexplained developmental delay and normal karyotype years ago; (2) a couple with three miscarriages — the father may carry a balanced translocation; (3) a pregnant patient whose cell-free DNA screen reports “high probability, trisomy 21”. Question token: “Which test answers each question — and what can each test NOT see?”

cues.text: Three requests reach the cytogenetics lab. A child with unexplained developmental delay. A couple with repeated miscarriages, where a parent may carry a balanced translocation.
And a pregnant patient whose cell-free DNA screen reports a high probability of trisomy 21.
Which test answers each question, and what is each test blind to?

props.label: Which test? What can it NOT see?

scenes.title: Three ways to look at chromosomes
scenes.altText: Three method cards. G-banded karyotype (GTG banding): a whole-genome snapshot of single cells in metaphase; detects numerical and structural changes including balanced translocations and inversions; limited to changes larger than about 5 Mb. FISH: fluorescent probes for chosen targets (whole-chromosome paints, centromere enumeration probes, locus-specific probes); interphase FISH works on non-dividing cells; it sees only what the probe targets. Chromosomal microarray (aCGH/SNP array): genome-wide copy-number measurement; resolution about 100 kb to 1 Mb, some arrays down to ~25 kb; SNP arrays also detect loss of heterozygosity and uniparental disomy.

cues.text: A G-banded karyotype looks at whole chromosomes in single dividing cells. It catches extra or missing chromosomes and structural changes, including balanced translocations and inversions, but only changes larger than about 5 megabases.

FISH uses fluorescent probes for chosen targets: whole-chromosome paints, centromere probes for counting, and locus-specific probes. Interphase FISH works on non-dividing cells, but it sees only what the probe targets.
A chromosomal microarray measures copy number across the whole genome, at about 100 kilobases to 1 megabase, and some arrays down to about 25 kilobases.
SNP arrays add one more view: loss of heterozygosity and uniparental disomy.

scenes.title: What each test cannot see
scenes.altText: Blind-spot cards. Microarray: measures copy number only, so truly balanced rearrangements are generally not detected, and low-level mosaicism may be missed (Miller 2010). Karyotype: submicroscopic deletions/duplications below its resolution are missed. FISH: anything outside the probe target is invisible. Yield card (ISCA consensus, Miller 2010): for unexplained developmental delay/intellectual disability, autism or multiple congenital anomalies, CMA yields 15–20% vs ~3% for G-banded karyotype; CMA recommended as the first-tier test; karyotype reserved for obvious chromosomal syndromes (e.g., Down syndrome), a family history of rearrangement, or multiple miscarriages.

cues.text: Every test has a blind spot. A microarray measures copy number only, so a truly balanced rearrangement, with nothing gained or lost, is generally invisible to it. Low-level mosaicism can also be missed.
A karyotype misses deletions and duplications too small to see under the microscope. FISH misses anything its probes do not target.

For unexplained developmental delay, intellectual disability, autism or multiple congenital anomalies, the 2010 consensus found microarray diagnosed 15 to 20 percent, versus about 3 percent for a karyotype, and recommended microarray as the first-tier test.
Karyotype stays first for obvious chromosomal syndromes such as Down syndrome, a family history of chromosome rearrangement, or multiple miscarriages: exactly where balanced translocations matter.

scenes.title: Calling a clone; confirming a screen
scenes.altText: Clone card (ISCN, as summarized by Wan 2014): a clone needs at least 2 cells with the same gain or structural rearrangement, or at least 3 cells with the same chromosome loss; a single abnormal cell is not reported as a clone. Prenatal card (Poulton & Hui 2025; Santoli 2025): cell-free DNA (NIPT) is a screening test from 10 weeks; false positives occur, partly from confined placental mosaicism (placenta aneuploid, fetus euploid); a high-probability result needs genetic counselling and confirmatory diagnostic testing by CVS or amniocentesis; microarray is recommended for fetal structural anomalies. Back to the hook: child → microarray; miscarriage couple → parental karyotype; cfDNA high probability → counselling + CVS/amniocentesis.

cues.text: In a culture, how many abnormal cells make a clone? A gain or a structural rearrangement must be seen in at least two cells; a loss in at least three. One odd cell is not reported as a clone.
Cell-free DNA testing, from 10 weeks of pregnancy, is a screening test. False positives happen, partly from confined placental mosaicism: the placenta is aneuploid but the fetus is not.
So a high-probability result needs genetic counselling and confirmation by chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis. For fetal structural anomalies, microarray is recommended.
Back to the requests: the child with developmental delay gets a microarray.
The miscarriage couple gets parental karyotypes to look for a balanced translocation, and the screen-positive pregnancy gets counselling and a diagnostic procedure.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Microarray detects balanced translocations” (✓ copy number only; balanced rearrangements need a karyotype); “One abnormal cell confirms mosaicism” (✓ a clone needs ≥ 2 cells with the same gain/structural change or ≥ 3 with the same loss); “A positive cfDNA screen is a diagnosis” (✓ screening only; confirm with CVS or amniocentesis).

cues.text: Trap one: a microarray detects balanced translocations. No: it measures copy number, and a balanced rearrangement gains or loses nothing. Use a karyotype.
Trap two: one abnormal cell confirms mosaicism. No: a clone needs at least two cells with the same gain or structural change, or three with the same loss.
Trap three: a positive cell-free DNA screen is a diagnosis. No: it is screening; confirm with chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis.

scenes.title: Arrays weigh, karyotypes look
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Arrays weigh, karyotypes look, FISH only finds what it fishes for.” A balance scale (array: more or less DNA), an eye (karyotype: arrangement), a fishing hook (FISH: one target). A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: arrays weigh, karyotypes look, and FISH only finds what it fishes for. An array weighs how much DNA is there; a karyotype looks at how it is arranged; FISH checks one chosen target.
Where it breaks: SNP arrays also detect loss of heterozygosity and uniparental disomy; karyotypes need dividing cells and can miss small changes; and resolution figures vary by platform and probe.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Karyotype: balanced changes, > ~5 Mb · FISH: probe targets only · CMA: copy number, first-tier for DD/ID, blind to balanced”, “Clone: gain/structural ≥ 2 cells, loss ≥ 3 · cfDNA = screening → CVS/amnio”.

cues.text: Choose the test by what it can see: microarray for copy number, karyotype for balanced rearrangements, FISH for a chosen target, and always confirm a positive cell-free DNA screen with a diagnostic test.

props.label: Karyotype: balanced, > ~5 Mb · FISH: probe only · CMA: copy number, blind to balanced
Clone: gain/structural ≥ 2 cells, loss ≥ 3 · cfDNA = screening → CVS/amnio

explanation.what: Plain language: different chromosome tests look at different things — a karyotype looks at how chromosomes are arranged, FISH checks chosen spots, and a microarray measures how much DNA is present everywhere. Scientific terms: G-banding (GTG), metaphase, FISH (whole-chromosome paint, centromere enumeration probe, locus-specific probe), chromosomal microarray (aCGH, SNP array), copy-number variant, balanced rearrangement, loss of heterozygosity, uniparental disomy, clone, cell-free DNA screening, confined placental mosaicism.
explanation.why: A balanced rearrangement changes arrangement without changing copy number, so only methods that look at chromosome structure (karyotype, targeted FISH) can see it. Small deletions/duplications fall below the light-microscope resolution of a karyotype but are measured by arrays. Cell-free DNA in maternal plasma is released from maternal cells and the placenta, so confined placental mosaicism can produce screen results that do not reflect the fetus.
explanation.measure: Karyotype: changes > ~5 Mb, balanced and unbalanced (Rohani 2018). aCGH: ~100 kb–1 Mb (Wan 2014); arrays down to ~25 kb (Rohani 2018). CMA diagnostic yield 15–20% vs karyotype ~3% for DD/ID, ASD, MCA; first-tier (Miller 2010). Clone: ≥ 2 cells with the same gain or structural rearrangement, ≥ 3 with the same loss (ISCN via Wan 2014). cfDNA from 10 weeks; high-probability results need counselling and CVS/amniocentesis (Poulton & Hui 2025).
explanation.differs: Karyotype (arrangement, balanced changes, dividing cells) vs microarray (copy number, higher resolution, blind to balanced changes) vs FISH (targeted, works in interphase). Screening (cfDNA) vs diagnostic testing (CVS, amniocentesis).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: which test detects a balanced translocation, first-tier test for developmental delay, clone cell-count rule, and what to do after a positive cell-free DNA screen.

right.label: Chromosomal microarray
points: Copy number at ~100 kb–1 Mb or better

comparisons.distinguisher: Balanced rearrangement suspected → karyotype; unexplained DD/ID/MCA → microarray.

comparisons.title: cfDNA screening vs diagnostic testing
comparisons.distinguisher: Only a diagnostic procedure confirms a high-probability screen.

mnemonic.text: Arrays weigh, karyotypes look, FISH only finds what it fishes for.
mnemonic.explanation: Microarray measures copy number (how much DNA); karyotype shows arrangement (including balanced changes); FISH detects only its probe target.
mnemonic.limitation: SNP arrays also detect LOH/UPD; karyotypes need dividing cells and miss small changes; resolution varies by platform and probe.

questions.stem: A couple has had three first-trimester miscarriages. Which test is most appropriate to look for a parental balanced translocation?

options.rationale: Correct. A karyotype shows chromosome arrangement and detects balanced translocations.
Incorrect. Microarray measures copy number; a truly balanced translocation gains or loses nothing.
Incorrect. cfDNA screens a pregnancy for aneuploidy; it does not examine parental chromosome structure.

options.text: Interphase FISH with a chromosome 21 centromere probe
options.rationale: Incorrect. A single enumeration probe counts one chromosome and would not reveal an unknown translocation.

questions.stem: In a 20-cell karyotype, one cell shows loss of chromosome 7 and the other 19 are normal. How should this be interpreted?

options.text: Not a clone; a single cell with a loss does not meet the clone definition
options.rationale: Correct. A loss must be seen in at least three cells to be called clonal.
Incorrect. One cell is not enough for any clone; a loss needs ≥ 3 cells.

options.text: Clonal if one more cell shows the same loss
options.rationale: Incorrect. Two cells suffice for a gain or structural change, not for a single chromosome loss.

options.text: Reflex to microarray to confirm a balanced rearrangement
options.rationale: Incorrect. Loss of a chromosome is not balanced, and microarray cannot see balanced changes anyway.

questions.stem: A cell-free DNA screen at 11 weeks reports “high probability of trisomy 21”. What is the appropriate next step?

options.text: Genetic counselling and diagnostic testing by CVS or amniocentesis
options.rationale: Correct. cfDNA is screening; false positives (e.g., confined placental mosaicism) occur, so a diagnostic test confirms.

options.text: Report the fetus as having Down syndrome
options.rationale: Incorrect. A screening result is not a diagnosis.

options.text: Repeat the cfDNA screen and act on two positives
options.rationale: Incorrect. Repeating a screen does not convert it into a diagnosis; placental mosaicism would persist.
Incorrect. Parental copy number does not diagnose the fetal karyotype.

claims.text: Karyotype detects balanced changes at > ~5 Mb; FISH probe types and interphase use; array resolution; SNP arrays detect LOH/UPD.
CMA blind to truly balanced rearrangements and low-level mosaicism; yield 15–20% vs ~3%; first-tier; karyotype for obvious syndromes, family rearrangement, multiple miscarriages.
Clone: ≥ 2 cells same gain/structural change, ≥ 3 cells same loss.
cfDNA is screening from 10 weeks; false positives incl. confined placental mosaicism; confirm with CVS/amniocentesis; microarray for fetal anomalies.
High-resolution karyotype ~3 Mb; FISH ~150 kb; score 15–20 cells; procedure timings, loss rates and NIPS accuracy.
